title: Merging & Sorting Linked Lists
summary: Merging sorted lists and adapting merge sort to a structure with no random access — why merge sort, not quicksort, is the list-native sorting algorithm.

slides.markdown:
Sorting an array and sorting a linked list are different problems in disguise, because the list gives up **random access** — the one thing quicksort's partitioning leans on hardest.

Merge sort, by contrast, needs only sequential access and a way to split a sequence roughly in half — both of which a linked list supports fine with a slow/fast pointer. That's why merge sort is the list-native sort, and why "sort a linked list" interview questions are really testing whether you notice the structure has changed the right algorithm to reach for.

Everything else here — merging two sorted lists, merging k of them, dedup, complex reordering — builds on the same merge primitive.

slides.sectionTitle: Why merge sort fits a list
slides.markdown:
Quicksort's partition step needs to compare an element against a pivot and swap it into place relative to elements on both sides — on an array that's O(1) index arithmetic, on a list it degenerates into repeated linear scans just to find "the element before this one" for swapping.

Merge sort needs exactly two list-friendly operations: **split** a sequence into two halves (a single fast/slow-pointer pass finds the midpoint, no indices needed) and **merge** two already-sorted sequences by repeatedly taking the smaller front element (pure pointer-following, no random access at all).

The recursion is identical to array merge sort — split, recurse, merge — but every step maps onto pointer operations the list already supports natively, which is the whole reason merge sort wins here.

slides.sectionTitle: Merging two sorted lists in place
Merge sort on a list vs on an array
slides.subTitle: What changes when you lose random access
slides.markdown:
| | Array merge sort | Linked-list merge sort |
|---|---|---|
| Split | O(1) index arithmetic | O(n) fast/slow pointer walk |
| Merge | needs a new output array, O(n) space | re-links existing nodes, O(1) extra space |
| Total extra space | O(n) | O(log n) — recursion stack only |
| Cache behavior | good (contiguous reads) | worse (pointer chasing) |

Counterintuitively, the list version uses **less** auxiliary space than the array version, because merging doesn't need a fresh buffer — you're just re-pointing existing nodes. What you lose is cache-friendliness: even though both are O(n log n), the array version usually wins on wall-clock time at the same n, for the same locality reasons that show up everywhere else in this group.

People sometimes try to force quicksort onto a linked list by picking a pivot and doing a single pass to build three sublists (less-than, equal, greater-than the pivot), then concatenating and recursing. This *can* work, but it quietly gives up quicksort's main real-world advantage.

Array quicksort's in-place partitioning is fast specifically because swapping two array slots is O(1) index arithmetic with excellent cache behavior. On a list there's nothing to "swap in place" — you're building new sublists by re-linking nodes one at a time, which is really just a different-shaped merge step wearing quicksort's name. And unlike merge sort, list quicksort has no easy way to guarantee balanced splits, so a bad pivot choice (already-sorted input, naively picking the first element) degrades to O(n²) with no in-place-swap benefit to offset it.

The practical takeaway: don't reach for quicksort on a list by default — reach for it only if a specific constraint (e.g., strict O(1) *extra* space beyond input, no recursion) rules out merge sort first.

slides.subTitle: Pairwise merging step by step
slides.markdown:
Given k sorted lists, one option is to merge them pairwise: merge list 1 with list 2, merge that result with list 3, and so on, one at a time. That costs O(nk) total, where n is the total node count across all lists, because the growing merged list gets re-scanned against every remaining list.

A better pairwise strategy merges lists in **rounds**, like a tournament bracket: round 1 merges (1,2), (3,4), (5,6)…, round 2 merges the round-1 results pairwise again, and so on, halving the list count each round. That's O(n log k) total — each of the log k rounds costs O(n) — because no single merge involves the full k-way comparison, only ever two lists at a time.

The heap-based alternative (maintain a size-k min-heap of list fronts) reaches the same O(n log k) bound with a different constant-factor profile — covered in the `heaps` group's k-way merge topic, which this problem is the canonical use case for.

slides.sectionTitle: Removing duplicates from a sorted list

slides.subTitle: L0→Ln→L1→Ln-1→…
slides.markdown:
Reordering a list so it alternates first-from-front, first-from-back (L0, Ln, L1, Ln-1, L2, Ln-2, …) looks like it needs random access to "the last element," "the second-to-last," and so on — which a singly linked list doesn't have.

The list-native solution combines three primitives already in this group: find the middle (fast/slow pointers), **reverse the second half** in place, then **merge the two halves by alternating nodes** — take one from the front half, one from the reversed second half, repeat.

This is the clearest example in the group of why learning the individual primitives pays off: nothing here is a new algorithm, it's three previously-learned techniques composed in sequence. Recognizing that composition, rather than inventing a fourth approach from scratch, is the actual skill being tested.

slides.sectionTitle: Where merge sort's guarantees actually matter
slides.markdown:
One property of list merge sort is worth naming explicitly in an interview: it's **stable** — equal-valued elements keep their original relative order — because the merge step always takes from the left list on ties (`if l1.val <= l2.val`).

This matters whenever you're sorting composite records by one field but need ties broken by insertion order (e.g., sorting log entries by timestamp where equal timestamps should stay in arrival order). Array quicksort commonly isn't stable without extra bookkeeping; list merge sort is stable for free, as a side effect of always preferring the left source on equality.

Worth remembering as the closing fact for this topic: reach for merge sort on a list not just because it's asymptotically fine, but because its natural implementation happens to give you stability at no extra cost.
